newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - New drugs mean hope for herpes, after all.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - New drugs mean hope for herpes, after all.

text.p: It was known ironically as "the gift that keeps on giving" -- a sexually transmitted disease that was painful, highly infectious -- and incurable.
Fifteen years after genital herpes transformed the sexual habits of singles on the Western dating scene, it remains an excruciating reminder of the perils of promiscuity.
It was knocked out of the headlines in the mid-1980s by AIDS which, with its fatal effects, is far more frightening. But herpes is on the rise.

A survey published earlier this month by the International Herpes Management Forum (IHMF), a committee of doctors who work with herpes patients, found incidences of genital herpes had increased 23 percent over the past decade in the United States.
One in five people there has it.
Surveys of blood tests indicated that 107 million people worldwide were infected with the HSV-2 virus that causes genital herpes. Of those, 80 percent did not know.
Of the 21.4 million who did know they had herpes, 73 percent had not been treated with any drugs.
DOCTORS NEED THE FACTS, EXPERTS SAY
Although herpes is still incurable, drugs have been developed that greatly reduce the pain and itching associated with the ugly blisters, and can prevent a break-out if taken quickly enough.
Doctors working with the forum say they are horrified that so few people know that herpes can be treated with drugs and are worried about the ignorance that persists about the condition.
"Doctors need to give people the facts," said Dr Simon Barton, director of Genito-Urinary Medicine at London's Chelsea and Westminster Hospital.
Symptoms can consist of stabbing pains, swollen glands or painful urination, and sometimes no blisters, making herpes hard to diagnose.

"I actually had no idea that my condition was genital herpes," said Curtis Phinney, a 40-year-old organic chemist living just outside Washington D.C. "I just knew that something was very, very wrong."
After suffering up to eight outbreaks a year, Phinney is now on drugs that have suppressed it completely.
"It takes time for people to hear about the guidelines," said Barton. "For patients who were told five years ago that there was no treatment, and are fed up, it's time to re-visit that issue."
A "BRAND, A DISGRACE, A REPROACH"
One of the worst things about herpes is that it is highly infectious -- and it can be passed on even when there is no evidence of an outbreak.

"It also has significant psychological and social effects," said Dr John Harris of St Mary's Hospital in London, who has studied herpes for 20 years. Victims become depressed, fear their sexual lives are over and worry about infecting partners.
Gay Baynes, a psychotherapist working with the IHMF, said sufferers felt angry, or contaminated. "It's a brand, a disgrace, a reproach," she said.
"Man, it's a shock," said "Paul" (not his real name), an Australian pilot who learned he was infected during a long-term faithful relationship. "It's absolutely devastating."

Paul said his biggest fear was that his daughters, aged seven and 11, could be infected through casual contact. "I thought I was going to pass this virus on to my kids," he said, his voice choking. "They were as pure as the driven snow."
Gonorrhea can be treated with penicillin, syphilis is a disease of the past, but every outbreak of herpes is a reminder.
"It's like an old girlfriend coming back to visit, every time you get in bed with someone," Harris said.
PHARMACEUTICAL COMPANIES RACE TO IMPROVE DRUGS

Related to chickenpox, cold sores and shingles, herpes simplex 2 is not life-threatening -- except to AIDS patients. Their damaged immune systems cannot withstand the virus, and doctors say it is vital to suppress it.

Drugs are available to do just that and experts see no reason why genital herpes and even cold sore victims cannot benefit. The first generation, which dominated the field for years, is aciclovir (Glaxo-Wellcome's Zovirax).

But aciclovir must be taken up to five times a day, every day, to suppress herpes. It is considered a very safe drug, with few side-effects, but it is expensive and inconvenient to take at such frequencies.
"I was taking five pills a day," Paul said. "You walk down the street and you're rattling."

Two new versions of aciclovir -- SmithKline Beecham's Famciclovir (Famvir) and Glaxo Wellcome's Valaciclovir (Valtrex) -- are absorbed better by the body and can be taken in lower doses. Both companies are seeking approval for one- or two-pill- a-day regimens.
"That is sort of a holy grail where genital herpes is concerned," said Dr Raj Patel, a specialist in genito-urinary medicine at Southampton University.
Despite the availability of such drugs, most doctors prescribe nothing at all, or perhaps Zovirax cream.
But Barton says this is inefficient.
"Most people don't actually see their genitals five times a day," Barton said. "And when you apply cream to your genitals it tends to keep soaking into your underwear."
The main goal is a vaccine that would cure sufferers, rather than just suppressing their symptoms.
Researchers have noted that people who have suffered cold sores have less of a chance of becoming infected with HSV-2.
"Millions and millions of man-hours are being spent on developing a vaccine because of that," Barton said.

But last November California biotechnology giant Chiron Corp announced that its once-promising genetically engineered vaccine for genital herpes was a failure. Cantab Pharmaceuticals of Cambridge, England is testing a vaccine using disabled infectious single cycle (DISC) viruses that its says combine the efficacy of attenuated, or partially disabled live viruses, with the safety of those using inactivated viruses.
Other experts are sceptical, but the vaccine is now in clinical trials.
